title: Pacing in Long-Distance Running: Sex and Age Differences in 10-km Race and Marathon
authors: Cuk I, Nikolaidis PT, Villiger E, Knechtle B
population: Official results of the Oslo marathon (n = 8,828) and 10-km race (n = 16,315), 2015 to 2018
findings: Both 10-km runners and marathoners showed positive pacing strategies (slower later in the race).
Women slowed less than men in the marathon (9.85% against 12.70%) but not in the 10-km race (3.99% against 3.38%).
Pace change was more marked in the youngest and the oldest marathoners than in the other age groups (12.55% against 10.96%).
limitations: Four editions of one city's events; results data only (no weather, effort or training); the abstract does not say how the slowing percentage is computed beyond 'positive pacing'.
implications: At 10 km the typical slowing is about 3 to 4%, against about 10 to 13% in the marathon, so a first-half pacing line is a marathon matter. Supports giving a 10 km goal the time, pace and heat blocks without a split or fade line.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Medicina 57:389). Abstract read on Europe PMC. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
